To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
older adults are less able than younger adults to perceive the position of the shoulder and the knee and the force produced by the hip extensors and the elbow flexors.

the elderly had a higher proprioceptive deficit in segmental positioning tests and in the reproduction of force at 20% and 30% of the maximum isometric contraction of the quadriceps and shoulder flexor muscles.
the elderly have a lower proprioceptive threshold for large-amplitude movements in the lower limbs and a lower proprioceptive sensitivity in reproducing small forces of the lower and upper limbs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the perception of joint position and force level in elderly and young subjects.
the study of the perception of position and of the level of force, in elderly and young people.
the effects of aging on the perception of body position and force.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the elderly have a lower proprioceptive capacity in the performance of movements of large amplitude for upper limbs and of low amplitude for lower limbs.

older adults are more susceptible to the loss of proprioceptive information and the ability to process that information, and this may have implications for their ability to maintain balance, and thus their risk for falls.
the older adults have a lower proprioceptive sensitivity, but this difference is not significant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the perception of joint position and of the level of force are affected in the elderly.
the elderly people have a lower perception of the articular positioning and the level of the force exerted.
the elderly have a reduced capacity for proprioception and force control.
